name: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan
role: President of Türkiye during the assessed period
description: Turkish president assessed through executive centralisation, religious conservatism and mixed market and state-directed policies.

axes.brief: Regular competitive elections persisted while executive centralisation, pressure on opposition and weakened checks constrained equal competition.
axes.counter: Accepted opposition victories in local elections; a failed military coup was rejected. Neither fully open competition nor unelected military rule describes the whole period.

axes.brief: Broad counterterrorism powers, media restrictions and coercive security policies prioritised state authority.
axes.counter: Some civil legal safeguards and ordinary criticism remained; court-authorised policing should not be conflated with every extrajudicial practice.

axes.brief: Turkish national identity and shared cultural-religious norms were emphasised, with restricted Kurdish political autonomy.
axes.counter: Large refugee populations and some minority worship recognition persisted; cultural assimilation does not automatically imply closed immigration.

axes.brief: Hosted millions of Syrian refugees while tightening management and encouraging returns by the late period.
axes.counter: Temporary protection is not guaranteed permanent settlement; economic, family and humanitarian routes differed from unconditional openness.

axes.brief: Military operations beyond the borders, defence industrial development and strategic coercion were prominent.
axes.counter: NATO participation, negotiations and diplomatic bargaining remained; autonomous lethal targeting is an uncertain technology-specific estimate.

axes.brief: Sovereign decision-making and resistance to external political judgments coexisted with NATO and trade ties.
axes.counter: Alliances and regional cooperation did not mean surrendering currency, border or final domestic legal authority.

axes.brief: Private enterprise and construction investment coexisted with state banks, strategic assets and public broadcasting.
axes.counter: Market participation is not a general commitment to divesting all state assets; industrial and financial control qualify a simple privatisation label.

axes.brief: International trade and investment were valued alongside strategic protection and domestic industrial priorities.
axes.counter: Tariffs, local procurement and strategic ownership restrictions coexist with export-led business; mixed estimates reflect policy rather than party identity.

axes.brief: Directed credit, unorthodox interest-rate pressure and industrial priorities steered a private-business economy.
axes.counter: Most firms still used markets and prices; central control of monetary priorities does not imply compulsory production quotas in every sector.

axes.brief: Social assistance, housing and minimum-wage support accompanied business-oriented development.
axes.counter: Benefits were often targeted and clientelist; support for poorer households is not a documented comprehensive wealth-equalisation programme.

axes.brief: Religious education, public religious institutions and Islamic social norms gained state support.
axes.counter: Türkiye retained civil courts and no constitutional clerical legislative veto; religious conservatism is not the same legal structure as Khomeini’s guardianship of the jurist.

axes.brief: Traditional family, gender roles, modesty and opposition to LGBT recognition were strongly emphasised.
axes.counter: Women’s public employment and elections continued; traditionalism does not determine every biological-causation answer.

axes.brief: Infrastructure, defence technology and industrial development were priorities.
axes.counter: Religious and regulatory constraints and clinical safeguards qualify unrestricted biomedical innovation; broad development policy does not settle enhancement risks.

axes.brief: Executive centralisation and replacement of elected municipal officials constrained regional authority.
axes.counter: Some municipal elections and local powers remained; recognition of local services is not regional constitutional sovereignty or secession.

axes.brief: Education, family and religious-social formation were invoked as influences on conduct, with traditional sex-role arguments.
axes.counter: None establishes an exact heredity model of intelligence, stress or empathy. Gender-role rhetoric weakly informs only the pay-gap estimate and is explicitly uncertain.
